title: Bactria
wiki_lead:
Bactria (; Bactrian: βαχλο, Bakhlo), or Bactriana, was an ancient civilization in Central Asia, located in the area south of the Oxus River (modern Amu Darya) and north of the  Hindu Kush mountains, within modern-day Afghanistan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Bactria was strategically located south of Sogdia and west of the Pamir Mountains. These mountain ranges acted as "walls" protecting Bactria from three sides, with the Pamir mountains to the north and the Hindu Kush to the south forming a junction, and the Karakoram range towards the east.
Called "beautiful Bactria, crowned with flags" in the Avesta, the region is considered, in the Zoroastrian faith, to be one of the "sixteen perfect Iranian lands" that the supreme deity, Ahura Mazda, had created. It was once a small and independent kingdom struggling to survive against nomadic Turanians. One of the early centres of Zoroastrianism, and capital of the legendary Kayanian dynasty, Bactria is mentioned in the Behistun Inscription of Darius the Great as one of the satrapies of the Achaemenid Empire; it was a special satrapy, ruled by a crown prince or an intended heir. Bactria was the centre of Iranian resistance against the Greek Macedonian invaders after the fall of the Achaemenid Empire in the 4th century BC, but eventually fell to Alexander the Great.
After the death of Alexander, Bactria fell to his general, Seleucus I. The Seleucids lost the region to the satrap Diodotus I, when he declared independence; thus marking the beginning of the Greco-Bactrian and Indo-Greek Kingdoms. By the 2nd century BC, Bactria was conquered by the Parthian Empire, and, in the early 1st century, by the Kushan Empire, believed to have been founded by the Yuezhi. Bactrian (natively known as ariao, 'Iranian'), an Eastern Iranian language, was the common language of Bactria and the surroundings areas, from ancient until early medieval times.
Shapur I, the second Sasanian King of Kings of Iran, conquered western parts of the Kushan Empire in the 3rd century, and the Kushano-Sasanian Kingdom was established. The Sasanians lost Bactria in the 4th century, but reconquered it in the 6th century.
The Islamization of Bactria began with the Muslim conquest of Iran in the 7th century. The capital city of Bactra was the centre of an Iranian Renaissance in the 8th and 9th centuries, and New Persian as an independent literary language first emerged in this region. The Samanid Empire was formed in Eastern Iran by the descendants of Saman Khuda, a Persian from Bactria, leading to the spread of the Persian language in the region, and the decline of Bactrian.

Etymology

The modern English name of the region is Bactria. Historically, the region was first mentioned in Avestan as Bakhdi in Old Persian. This later developed into Bāxtriš in Middle Persian and Baxl in New Persian. The modern name is derived from the Ancient Greek: Βακτριανή (Romanized Greek term: Baktrianē), which is the Hellenized version of the Bactrian endonym. Other cognates include βαχλο (Romanized: Bakhlo). بلخ (Romanized: Balx), Chinese 大夏 (pinyin: Dàxià), Latin Bactriana. The region was mentioned in ancient Sanskrit texts as बाह्लीक or Bāhlīka.
Wilhelm Eilers proposed that the region was named after the Balkh River (in Greek transliteration Βάκτρος) from underlying Bāxtri-, itself meaning 'she who divides', from the Proto-Indo-European root *bhag- 'to divide' (whence also Avestan bag- and Old Indic bháj-).
Bactria is the geographic location after which Bactrian camels are named.


History


Bronze Age

The Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex (BMAC, also known as the "Oxus civilization") is the modern archaeological designation for a Bronze Age archaeological culture of Central Asia, dated to c. 2200–1700 BC, located in present-day eastern Turkmenistan, northern Afghanistan, southern Uzbekistan and western Tajikistan, centred on the upper Amu Darya (known to the ancient Greeks as the Oxus River), an area covering ancient Bactria. grok_lead: Bactria was an ancient region in Central Asia, roughly corresponding to parts of modern-day northern Afghanistan, southern Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan, situated between the Hindu Kush mountains to the south and the Amu Darya (Oxus River) to the north. Known for its fertile alluvial plains and strategic location at the crossroads of major trade routes, including the Silk Road, it served as a vital hub connecting regions from China to India and the Mediterranean. The region's capital, Bactra (modern Balkh), was renowned in antiquity as the "mother of cities" for its wealth, antiquity, and agricultural bounty, including grapes, oranges, water lilies, and a superior breed of camels. Historically, Bactria emerged as a significant satrapy within the Achaemenid Persian Empire, named as such by Cyrus the Great around 530 BCE and firmly incorporated by Darius I circa 520 BCE, as recorded in the Behistun Inscription. It was celebrated for its fierce Bactrian warriors, who fought in Persian armies, including at the Battle of Plataea in 480 BCE under Xerxes I, and for its deep ties to Zoroastrianism, with tradition holding it as the birthplace of the prophet Zoroaster (Zarathustra) in the second millennium BCE. The region featured ancient sanctuaries, such as one dedicated to the goddess Anahita in Bactra, and was linked to the Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex (circa 2200â1700 BCE), associated with early Indo-Iranian cultures. Bactria's prominence escalated during the Hellenistic era following its conquest by Alexander the Great in 329 BCE, after which it became a center for Greek-Macedonian settlement and cultural fusion at the northeastern edge of his empire. Under Seleucid rule, cities like AÃ¯ Khanum were founded around 300 BCE as outposts of Greek civilization, blending Corinthian architecture with local traditions until the site's destruction circa 145 BCE. Independence came around 250 BCE when Diodotus I established the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom, seceding from the weakening Seleucid Empire and fostering a prosperous era of coinage, trade, and artistic innovation that influenced neighboring India and China. The kingdom endured until circa 130 BCE, when invasions by the Yuezhi led to its fall, paving the way for Yuezhi control around 130 BCE and the subsequent rise of the Kushan Empire in the 1st century CE. In later centuries, Bactriaâevolving into Tokharistan âremained a cultural melting pot, embracing Buddhism under the Kushans and serving as a Silk Road conduit for silk, spices, and ideas until Arab conquests in 645 CE shifted it toward Islamic scholarship during the Samanid era (9thâ10th centuries). Archaeological treasures, such as the Bactrian Gold hoard from Tillya Tepe (discovered 1978) and artifacts from AÃ¯ Khanum (excavated 1964), underscore its role in bridging Eastern and Western civilizations, though much was lost to Mongol destruction in 1220 CE under Genghis Khan.
